name: Credential provider role (third party password and passkey manager)
plain: An app registers as the person's password and passkey manager for the whole system.
meaning: The chosen manager can supply logins for every other app and site, and sees which services the person signs into. It is one of the most trusted roles on the phone.

android.prompt_ui: User picks provider in Settings > Passwords & accounts
android.store_policy: Play: credential manager apps follow User Data policy
android.note: Provider apps must be enabled by the user; Android 15 adds default-provider behaviors.

ios.prompt_ui: Settings > General > AutoFill & Passwords picks apps
ios.note: iOS 17 adds passkey providers; iOS 26 adds credential exchange.

limits.headline: Can act as your phone's password and passkey manager once you turn it on
limits.user_action: You open Settings and choose this app as your passwords and passkeys provider
can: Save passwords and passkeys that other apps and sites ask to store
Offer matching logins when you sign in to another app or website
Unlock a login after checking your fingerprint, face or master password
Offer passkeys to other apps and sites on iPhone from iOS 17
cannot: Become your provider until you turn it on in Settings
See logins stored by other providers
Hand over a login without your approval on screen
Work in apps that block autofill
limits.reach_label: Every login you store with it
limits.differs: Android has a system role and a default provider choice. iPhone has an Autofill provider switch and added passkey support in iOS 17.

story.what_it_is: An app becomes your phone's main place for passwords and passkeys.

marketing.name: Credential Manager providers
marketing.pitch: Android lets password managers plug in so you can sign in with passkeys and passwords from your chosen app.

marketing.name: Passwords and passkeys providers
marketing.pitch: Apple lets other password apps supply logins and passkeys system wide, alongside its own Passwords app.

story.for_you: You pick a manager in Settings and from then on it offers your logins in every app and website. You also see its name at sign in. It feels like one safe place for all your accounts.
story.for_makers: For a password manager this role is the product: it is how its logins show up everywhere without copy and paste. It is also the most trusted job on a phone, because it can see which services you use.

use_cases.example: A password app fills your work login in a banking app, a news app and a browser, all from one unlock.
A manager shows you only the passkey for the real site and warns you that a look alike site has none saved.
You sign back into a game on a new phone and your manager fills the login and the one time code in a single step.
A company rolls out one approved manager to staff phones so every work app signs in the same way.
A family plan lets a parent share one safe login with a child's phone without typing the password in front of them.
Your bank app asks to create a passkey, and your chosen manager stores it and syncs it to your tablet.

story.android_note: Android treats this as a switch in Settings, and you can have more than one provider with one set as the main.
story.ios_note: iPhone lets third party managers act as the system provider, and the user turns them on in Settings under Passwords.

technical_bounds: User chooses provider explicitly in Settings on both OS

history.change: Password manager extensions as AutoFill providers
